nameStory: Wax myrtle gets its name from the waxy coating on its berries, which early colonists discovered could be boiled to extract wax for making candles. This natural wax burned cleaner and smelled much better than smoky animal fat candles, making bayberry candles a prized luxury. The tradition of burning bayberry candles on New Year's Eve for good luck continues today!
description: Wax myrtle is an evergreen shrub or small tree that keeps its leaves year-round, making it stand out in New England's mostly deciduous landscape. It typically grows 6-20 feet tall with a dense, rounded shape and narrow, leathery leaves. This southern native is quite rare in New England, found only in the warmest coastal areas where it can survive the winters. Its small, waxy gray berries cluster along the branches and give the plant its distinctive appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, leathery evergreen leaves that feel thick and waxy to the touch, with small resin dots that release a spicy, aromatic scent when crushed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small gray berries covered in a thick, waxy coating that feels greasy when rubbed between your fingers, clustered tightly along the stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Evergreen shrub or small tree with dense branching, staying green through winter when most other plants are bare

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark that becomes slightly furrowed with age, often with multiple stems growing from the base

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers in small clusters that appear before the berries, easily missed without close inspection

habitat: In New England, wax myrtle is extremely rare and found only in the warmest coastal areas of southern New England, particularly sandy soils near the ocean. It thrives in salt-tolerant conditions and well-drained soils where winters are mild enough for this southern species to survive. Look for it in coastal shrublands, dune edges, and protected maritime forests.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright green shoots, and tiny inconspicuous flowers bloom in small clusters along the branches.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain dark green and waxy, while small berries begin forming and developing their characteristic waxy coating.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to their full gray, waxy appearance and become most noticeable on the evergreen branches as other plants lose their leaves.
seasonality.winter: Remains fully evergreen when most plants are bare, making it very conspicuous, with waxy berries persisting on branches through the cold months.

funFact: The wax from bayberry bushes was so valuable to colonial Americans that bayberry candles cost more than silver of the same weight, making them the ultimate luxury item that only the wealthy could afford for special occasions!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative northern bayberry, but northern bayberry drops its leaves in winter while wax myrtle stays evergreen year-round. Memory trick: 'Wax stays, northern goes' - the waxy one keeps its leaves through winter.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'southern' wax myrtle in much of its range, in New England it's simply wax myrtle since it represents the northern edge of this species' range. The extremely low observation count reflects its rarity this far north - you're seeing a plant at the very limits of where it can survive.
compareHints: Unlike its close relative northern bayberry which is deciduous and common throughout New England, wax myrtle is evergreen and extremely rare in the region. Northern bayberry has similar waxy berries and leaf shape, but drops all its leaves in fall, while wax myrtle keeps its thick, leathery leaves through the harshest winters. The evergreen nature makes wax myrtle unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern bayberry differs from its southern cousin, wax myrtle, by being deciduous (losing its leaves in winter) while wax myrtle is evergreen.
